samples.text:
In the last few years, extreme weather such as floods and heatwaves are happening more often in many countries. These events create a lot of difficulties for local communities. This essay will look at these problems and how communities can be more prepared.

The first problem is damage to homes and buildings. When there is a big flood, water enter into houses and destroys furniture and electrical things, and some families lose everything. Roads and bridges can also be broken, so people cannot go to work or school for many days. The second problem is health. During a heatwave, old people and small children can become very ill because of the high temperature, and some of them even die. After floods, the water is often dirty and it can spread diseases. In addition, farmers can lose their crops, and this make food more expensive for the whole community.

However, communities can prepare better for these events. One way is to build stronger infrastructure, for example flood walls and better drainage systems in the cities. Also, the local government should not allow people to build new houses in areas which flood very often. Another way is to give people information. If there is a good warning system on the phone and on television, people will have time to leave their homes before the flood arrive. For heatwaves, towns can open cool public buildings where old people can stay during the hottest part of day.

In conclusion, extreme weather causes damage to property, health problems and loss of crops. I think the best way to be prepare is to have strong infrastructure and a good warning system, so communities can protect theirselves.
samples.why: Both questions answered with relevant problems and preparations · limited development of ideas · basic but clear paragraphing · adequate vocabulary with some imprecision (electrical things) · several agreement, preposition and word-form errors.

samples.text:
As the climate changes, extreme weather events like floods, storms and heatwaves are occurring with increasing frequency in many regions. These events pose serious challenges for local communities, but careful planning can significantly reduce their impact.

The most immediate problem is the physical damage that such events cause. Floods can destroy homes, businesses and essential infrastructure within hours, leaving families homeless and cutting off access to hospitals, schools and workplaces. Rebuilding is often slow and expensive, and in poorer communities where few people have insurance, the financial losses can take years to recover from. Extreme heat creates a different but equally serious threat to public health. Elderly people, young children and those with existing medical conditions are especially vulnerable, and hospitals can quickly become overwhelmed during a prolonged heatwave. Furthermore, both floods and droughts can devastate local agriculture, which affects farmers' incomes and pushes up food prices for everyone.

Communities can prepare more effectively in several ways. First of all, investment in protective infrastructure, such as flood barriers, improved drainage and buildings designed to stay cool, would reduce the damage when disasters strike. Planning authorities should also stop approving new housing on floodplains, which only increase the number of people at risk. Secondly, early warning systems are essential. Sending alerts directly to mobile phones gives residents time to move valuables, evacuate or check on vulnerable neighbours. Finally, local councils could prepare detailed emergency plans, for example by identifying cooling centres for heatwaves and organising volunteers who know which residents live alone and might need help.

In conclusion, extreme weather threatens people's homes, health and livelihoods. By combining stronger infrastructure, sensible planning and effective warning systems, communities can become far more resilient to these growing risks.
samples.why: Clear position · problems and preparation measures extended with relevant examples · clear central idea in each paragraph · good range of vocabulary (floodplains, resilient) · mostly error-free with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Floods, storms and prolonged heatwaves, once regarded as rare events, are now a recurring feature of life in many parts of the world. Their consequences for local communities are wide-ranging, affecting property, health and livelihoods, but much of the harm can be mitigated if communities invest in preparation rather than simply reacting after disaster strikes.

The most tangible impact is the destruction of homes and infrastructure. A single severe flood can render entire streets uninhabitable, sever transport links and knock out power and water supplies, isolating residents from essential services. The costs of recovery fall disproportionately on low-income households, which are less likely to be insured and more likely to live in vulnerable locations. Heatwaves, though less visibly destructive, can be even more deadly. Prolonged high temperatures place severe strain on older people and those with chronic illnesses, particularly in densely built urban areas where heat is retained overnight. There are also slower economic consequences: repeated crop failures erode farmers' livelihoods, and small businesses forced to close again and again may never reopen.

Preparation must therefore operate on several levels. Physical adaptation is the foundation, from flood defences and permeable drainage to building codes that require better insulation and shading. Land-use planning matters just as much, since continuing to build on floodplains simply multiplies future losses. Infrastructure alone is insufficient, however, without effective communication. Reliable early warning systems, delivered through mobile networks and local media, give residents time to act, while clearly marked evacuation routes ensure that warnings translate into safety. Finally, strong community networks can make a decisive difference. Neighbourhood schemes that identify isolated or elderly residents, together with designated cooling centres, help ensure that the most vulnerable are not overlooked.

In conclusion, extreme weather damages property, endangers health and undermines local economies. Communities that combine resilient infrastructure, prudent planning and well-organised warning and support systems will be far better equipped to withstand these growing threats.
samples.why: Both parts sufficiently addressed with extended, well-supported ideas · preparation discussed at several levels in logical sequence · wide, precise vocabulary (render uninhabitable, permeable drainage) · varied, accurate complex sentences.
